points.description: Mentions comparing/fixing a constant mass of one element (e.g. same mass of element A) when looking at different compounds.
States that the law is based on mass data: the masses of the other element that combine with the fixed mass are measured/compared.
States that the same elements can combine to form more than one different compound.
States that the masses of the other element are in simple whole-number (integer) ratios, e.g. 1:2 or 2:3.
Explains that whole-number ratios imply matter is discrete/indivisible: elements combine in whole units, never fractions of a unit.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if whole-number ratios are linked to fixed or discrete amounts but the reasoning for indivisibility is not clear.

points.description: Concludes that the indivisible unit of mass/matter of an element is the atom, so matter is made of atoms.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if atoms are mentioned but not clearly identified as the indivisible unit of each element's mass.

rubric.notes: Equivalent wording and correct examples (e.g. carbon oxides, CO and CO2) earn marks. Full marks need the chain: fixed mass and data, multiple compounds, whole-number ratios, discreteness, atoms. Do not require exact wording.
